title: Impacts of wind farms on surface air temperatures

settings.description: Combined field-data and regional-model assessment of how utility-scale wind farms affect near-surface air temperature.

San Gorgonio, California field campaign of 18 June to 9 August 1989 over a farm of 23 m turbines with 8.5 m blades in 41 rows spaced 120 m apart, sampled only when wind blew perpendicular to the slope.
The upwind meteorological tower at 33.896 N, 116.604 W, elevation 290 m, measuring 5 m air temperature.
The downwind meteorological tower at 33.875 N, 116.562 W, elevation 214 m.
Vertical temperature profiles from Edwards Air Force Base during June-August 1989, at 4 AM, 10 AM and 4 PM.
RAMS control simulations with the wind turbine parameterization off, one hour long, initialised from 153 WMO soundings across four seasons and 21 western US stations.
Paired RAMS simulations with the rotor parameterization on for a 7x3 array of 100 m turbines with 100 m rotor diameter spaced 1 km apart.
Simulations stratified by positive 0-300 m potential temperature lapse rate, that is stable conditions.
Simulations stratified by negative lapse rate, that is unstable conditions.
Simulations stratified by mean ambient hub-height wind speed from below 2 m/s to above 20 m/s.
Simulations stratified by mean background lower-ABL turbulent kinetic energy from the control runs.
Simulations stratified by mean background surface kinetic energy dissipation rate, with thresholds at 2.7 and 6 W/m2.
Sensitivity ensembles with rotor-added turbulent kinetic energy set to 0, 0.5, 1, 2, 5, 10 and 15 m2/s2, each with 153 simulations.
Global land surface kinetic energy dissipation computed from the 25-year six-hourly JRA25 reanalysis on a 2.5 degree grid with 41 vertical levels.

claims.from: downwind location within the wind farm at night and early morning
claims.to: near-surface air temperature relative to upwind
claims.statement: Near-surface air temperatures downwind of the wind farm are higher than upwind during night and early morning hours.

claims.from: downwind location within the wind farm during the rest of the day
claims.to: near-surface air temperature relative to upwind
claims.statement: For the rest of the day the reverse holds, so the wind farm cools downwind near-surface air relative to upwind.

claims.from: Mann-Whitney rank sum testing of the downwind minus upwind signal
claims.statement: The observed temperature signal is statistically significant for most hours of the day, with the strongest significance in the afternoon cooling hours.
claims.match_note: Not extracted, so the extracted diurnal claims carry no confidence information.

claims.from: observed lapse rate sign at Edwards Air Force Base
claims.to: sign of the observed wind farm temperature signal
claims.statement: A positive lapse rate at 4 AM and negative lapse rates at 10 AM and 4 PM correspond to observed warming at 4 AM and cooling at 10 AM and 4 PM.
claims.match_note: Not extracted. This observational link between stability and the sign of the effect is the paper's key conditioning fact.

claims.from: wind farm rotor parameterization under positive lapse rate
claims.statement: In the simulations wind turbine rotors create warming under positive lapse rates.

claims.from: wind farm rotor parameterization under negative lapse rate
claims.statement: In the simulations wind turbine rotors create cooling under negative lapse rates.

claims.from: wider observed wind speed range under stable conditions
claims.to: scatter in the simulated temperature change
claims.statement: There is more scatter in the temperature change under positive lapse rates because the range of wind speeds is much wider under stable conditions.

claims.from: ambient hub-height wind speed below 2 m/s
claims.to: magnitude of the near-surface temperature change
claims.statement: The temperature signal becomes zero at hub-height wind speeds less than 2 m/s.

claims.from: ambient hub-height wind speed above 20 m/s
claims.to: magnitude of the near-surface temperature change
claims.statement: The temperature signal becomes zero at hub-height wind speeds greater than 20 m/s.

claims.from: ambient hub-height wind speed near 12 m/s
claims.to: magnitude of the near-surface temperature change
claims.statement: The temperature signal peaks at approximately 12 m/s hub-height wind speed, following a Gaussian shape.

claims.from: rotor cut-out above 20 m/s and intermittent operation
claims.statement: Above 20 m/s the rotors are designed to stop, so they work only intermittently and the mean surface temperature impact falls.

claims.from: high ambient turbulent kinetic energy
claims.to: magnitude of the near-surface temperature change
claims.statement: Temperature effects are large when ambient turbulent kinetic energy is small and small when it is large, because a well-mixed profile gains little from additional rotor mixing.

claims.from: background surface kinetic energy dissipation rate above 2.7 W/m2
claims.statement: The rotor impact starts to decrease once the background surface kinetic energy dissipation rate exceeds 2.7 W/m2.

claims.from: background surface kinetic energy dissipation rate above 6 W/m2
claims.statement: The rotor impact becomes almost zero at dissipation rates higher than 6 W/m2.

claims.from: rotor-generated wake turbulent kinetic energy
claims.statement: Rotors that generate more turbulence in their wakes have a stronger impact on near-surface air temperatures.
claims.match_note: Not extracted. This is the paper's first mitigation lever.

claims.from: rotor-generated wake turbulence
claims.to: kinetic energy available to downstream turbines
claims.statement: Turbulence generation draws on the kinetic energy of the mean flow, so higher-turbulence rotors further reduce the energy available to downstream turbines.

claims.from: rotor-generated turbulent kinetic energy between 0 and 0.5 m2/s2
claims.statement: Absorbed power increases for rotor turbulence between 0 and 0.5 m2/s2 and decreases thereafter, because a small wake turbulence triggers beneficial entrainment before consumption outweighs replenishment.
claims.match_note: Not extracted. A non-monotonic optimum, exactly the kind of relationship the counting rules require to be preserved.

claims.from: simulated ABL turbulent kinetic energy
claims.statement: Simulated ABL turbulent kinetic energy and surface kinetic energy dissipation rate are strongly correlated at r = 0.9475, which justifies using dissipation as a turbulence proxy.
claims.match_note: Not extracted, so the substitution underlying the global siting map is unsupported in the graph.

claims.from: global land surface in the JRA25 reanalysis
claims.to: mean surface kinetic energy dissipation rate
claims.statement: The global average surface kinetic energy dissipation is estimated at 2.1 W/m2.

claims.from: high topography such as the Rockies, Andes, Himalayas and Tibetan Plateau
claims.statement: Surface kinetic energy dissipation is high over high topography, which together with accessibility rules those regions out for wind farms.

claims.from: regions with background surface dissipation above the 3 W/m2 contour
claims.statement: Large parts of North and Central America, southern South America, northern Europe, Russia, northern China, the Rift Valley, southern Africa, southern Australia and New Zealand are identified as suitable for low-impact wind farms.
claims.match_note: Not extracted. The paper's siting recommendation, which is its most directly actionable output, is absent.

claims.from: the low-impact siting map
claims.statement: The low-impact map overlaps considerably with published wind resource maps, making the US Great Plains and Midwest attractive on both criteria.

claims.from: turbulence generated in rotor wakes enhancing vertical mixing
claims.to: sign of the near-surface temperature change under a given lapse rate
claims.statement: Enhanced vertical mixing brings warm air down under a positive lapse rate and cool air down under a negative lapse rate, which explains the observed diurnal sign reversal.
claims.match_note: Not extracted, so the extracted warming and cooling records stand without the mechanism that reconciles them.
